A sales manager in Hangzhou did Chinese RMB 100 million in revenue in a single year during COVID by selling protective equipment.

When I heard this story, it wasn't from the sales manager herself.

It was from her boss. And the way he told it? He couldn't stop smiling.

That moment stuck with me. Because in my experience, how a boss talks about their people tells you almost everything you need to know.

* * *

I have a friend who spent over two decades as a senior executive in multinationals before joining a Chinese private company. He shared an observation that I keep coming back to.

In the MNC world, he had a simple rule for reading leaders:

The good ones say "Follow me." The average ones say "Go."

One walks alongside the team. The other sends people in and watches from behind.

Simple. And it worked — for twenty years.

But when he joined a Chinese company, that rule stopped working.

* * *

Here's why.

Many Chinese business founders built their companies from scratch, with their own hands. Being hands-on isn't a weakness — it's often how they survived. So "Follow me" can mean genuine leadership, or it can just mean a founder who can't let go.

What he noticed instead was something more telling: what the boss talks about when they really get going.

He saw two kinds of bosses.

The first kind lights up when talking about themselves — their early hustle, the deals they closed, the obstacles they overcame. Ask them about their team? They give you a name or two. Move on quickly.

The second kind mentions their own story almost in passing. But ask about their people — and suddenly they're leaning forward, full of details, genuinely proud.

He told me: following the first kind is exhausting. Not because the work is hard. Because you're always reading the room, watching their mood, managing up.

Following the second kind? You actually have room to grow.

* * *

I've seen this play out up close.

A founder I know in Shenzhen — every time we meet, he leads with his team. Recently it was a sales rep who closed several major accounts within six months, worth tens of millions in RMB. He described it in detail. You'd think he was talking about his own kid acing an exam.

Another founder in Shanghai told me about an employee who never seemed that busy — but consistently topped the monthly sales rankings. When he looked closer, he found out why: this person had built up nearly 5,000 targeted connections on LinkedIn over the years. Quietly. Methodically. Long before anyone else thought to.

The Shanghai founder told me this with real admiration in his voice.

Both of these bosses? Their people tend to stick around. And they tend to do well.

* * *

So if you're a global professional considering working with or for a Chinese company, here's my honest suggestion:

Don't just evaluate the company. Sit down with the boss. And ask them two questions:

1\. "How did you build the business?"2\. "Who on your team are you most proud of — and why?"

Then listen carefully.

If they talk about themselves with passion but go vague when it comes to their people — take your time before deciding.

If they gloss over their own story but come alive when they talk about someone on their team — that's a boss worth following.

* * *

The best leaders I've observed aren't the ones with the most impressive personal story.

They're the ones who get more excited about your story than their own.

That's not a small thing. That's the whole thing.

* * *

Have you worked with a boss like this — either kind? I'd love to hear your experience in the comments.

In the past year or two, I've been getting more and more messages like these.

Most come from overseas students and professionals interested in China, or people who already have some contact with Chinese companies.

They usually get straight to the point:

"Can you recommend jobs in China?"

Or

"How can I work with Chinese companies?"

I usually don't start by answering about jobs, platforms, or visas.

I ask a simpler question first:

### Why China?

Why not Singapore? Why not Malaysia? Why not Vietnam? Why not stay in your home country and find Asia-related opportunities there?

What's interesting is that many people's first reaction is:

"Actually, other countries would work too."

This one sentence says a lot.

It shows they haven't really thought through "Why Work with China." They just have a vague sense that "Asia has opportunities," "China is growing fast," "I hear there are lots of opportunities."

This is trend perception, not strategic choice.

Among the international talent I've worked with over the years, those who truly commit to long-term China-related careers almost never make decisions casually.

They usually start by thinking through a deeper question:

Am I looking for a short-term job location, or am I choosing my position in a long-term opportunity network?

If you're also thinking about whether to Work with China, I suggest you take some time to answer a few questions first.

1 List 3 countries or regions in Asia you're interested in. For each, write down specifically "why."

2 Then ask yourself: if this reason didn't exist, would I still choose it?

3 Talk to 2 people who are already there. See what their real experience is like.

Understanding "why" matters more than understanding "how."

Because direction is more important than speed.

A European Marketing VP I know works for a Chinese multinational with nearly USD 1B in annual revenue.

During the annual strategy meeting he attended in Shanghai headquarters, the owner boss delivered a fiery speech: “This year, we will take 20% of European market share.”

The KPIs were already on the giant screen. Then the VP said calmly: “This plan violates local privacy regulations. We can’t do this.”

The room went silent for 5 seconds.

The twist came hours later at dinner. After a few glasses of Chinese yellow wine, a Chinese VP pulled him aside: “You’re right. But there’s a smarter way to tell him."

Say it as: "In my previous global roles, we ran into a similar issue."

He tried again by using the strategy he learnt. The boss nodded repeatedly: “Good. You see the bigger picture.”

Well, it might because the yellow wine works.

But what I want to say is saying No is not rejection. It’s the ability to get things done without breaking trust.

Below are a few patterns—based on my experience with Chinese bosses and executives. They reflect the cultural logic behind saying No in China's business context.

### 01\. “Customs” persuade better than “Rules”

Don’t say: “We can’t do this.” “This violates policy.”

Say instead: “In Europe, the usual practice is…”

“Other companies I worked with ran into problems because…”

Chinese leaders rarely resist expertise. They resist being proven wrong in front of others. Experience persuades better than directives.

### 02\. Boundaries must come after you’ve proven you can “fight”

In China, boundaries require earning trust first.

Show first that you can take ownership, carry weight, and deliver under pressure. Then, when you raise boundaries, the boss actually listens.

Cross-cultural trust is hard to build, but worth continuous efforts from the very first minute.

### 03\. Turn your No into: “I’m protecting you.”

Transform refusal into concern: “I worry this risk will eventually fall on you.” “The authority might challenge this later, it will heavily impact our reputation there.”

To many Chinese bosses, loyalty + risk awareness matter more than simply being “right.”

### 04\. Find a Chinese colleague who understands both you and the boss

Chinese companies have a unique structure: The org chart is visible, but the power logic is not.

You need a “translator”—not for language translation, but for:

### 05\. A “conditional Yes” is safer than a direct No

Chinese bosses love saying: “Let’s try first.” Saying No immediately can be seen as rigid.

Try this instead: “If A/B/C conditions are met, I’m happy to push forward. If not, the risk becomes too high.”

You appear flexible yet responsible. And often, the boss will quietly drop the idea themselves.

### 06\. Use fewer formal emails; use more WeChat and in-person clarity

In the West: email = primary communication channel.

In China, the order is: WeChat/Call → In-person → Email recap

Email is for confirming shared understanding, not for rejecting proposals. A “No” lands better in conversation than in a written record.

### Final Thoughts

Chinese bosses are not a single stereotype. Like leaders everywhere, they vary widely:

some bold, some cautious

some emotional, some analytical

some welcome challenge, some absolutely don’t

There is no one-fit-for-all formula. Your job is not to memorize techniques, but to read the person in front of you.

If your Chinese boss is reasonable and welcomes debate—great. You can be more direct.

But saying No is never the goal.

Aligning on the same Northern Star is. Protecting them—and yourself—while building a long-term working rhythm is the real skillset we need to build.

And of course, the most advanced skill is you don't need to say out that No, the boss says the No from his own mouth on your behalf.
